children.label: a
children.prompt: Why is it impossible to take the triangle on the left to the triangle on the right without using a reflection?

answer.short: The triangles have opposite orientations. Rotations and translations preserve orientation; a reflection reverses it.
answer.worked: Reading the interior angles from largest to smallest goes clockwise around the left triangle and anticlockwise around the right triangle. Rotations and translations preserve this order, while reflections reverse it. Therefore a reflection is required.

inlines.text: For parts (b)–(e), show that the triangle on the left can be taken to the triangle on the right using:
a rotation followed by a reflection

answer.short: Rotate $90^\circ$ anticlockwise about the left triangle’s right-angle vertex, then reflect in the vertical line 1.5 grid units to its right.
answer.worked: Let $C$ be the left triangle’s right-angle vertex. Rotate the triangle $90^\circ$ anticlockwise about $C$. Its long leg now points upwards and its short leg points left. Reflect in the vertical line 1.5 grid units to the right of $C$. This places the right-angle vertex three units to the right of its starting point, with the long leg upwards and the short leg to the right, matching the target triangle.

children.label: c
children.prompt: a reflection followed by a rotation

answer.short: Reflect in the vertical line 1.5 grid units to the right of the left triangle’s right-angle vertex, then rotate $90^\circ$ clockwise about the image of that vertex.
answer.worked: Let $C$ be the left triangle’s right-angle vertex. Reflect the triangle in the vertical line 1.5 grid units to the right of $C$. The image of $C$ is now the target right-angle vertex; the long leg points left and the short leg points upwards. Rotate $90^\circ$ clockwise about the image of $C$. The long leg then points upwards and the short leg points right, matching the target triangle.

children.label: d
children.prompt: a reflection followed by a translation

answer.short: Reflect in the line rising to the right at $45^\circ$ to the horizontal through the left triangle’s rightmost vertex, then translate one grid unit right and two grid units up.
answer.worked: Let $A$ be the left triangle’s rightmost vertex. Reflect in the line through $A$ rising to the right at $45^\circ$ to the horizontal. The horizontal long leg becomes vertical, and the vertical short leg becomes horizontal. Translate the reflected triangle one grid unit right and two grid units up. Its vertices then coincide with those of the target triangle.

children.label: e
children.prompt: a translation followed by a reflection.

answer.short: Translate three grid units right, then reflect in the line rising to the right at $45^\circ$ to the horizontal through the translated right-angle vertex.
answer.worked: Translate the left triangle three grid units right. Its right-angle vertex now coincides with the target right-angle vertex. Reflect in the line through this vertex rising to the right at $45^\circ$ to the horizontal. This exchanges the horizontal and vertical legs, placing the long leg upwards and the short leg to the right, matching the target triangle.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Remarkably, every rotation can be achieved with two reflections. To show this, consider two lines that intersect at $O$. The measure of the angle between the two lines is $\theta$. A point $P_0$ is reflected in the first line to $P_1$ and then in the second line to $P_2$. Show that this is a rotation by identifying the angle and centre of the rotation. Explain why this implies any rotation can be achieved with two reflections.

spec.description: Two dashed reflection lines meet at O. The horizontal line is followed by the rising line; their angle is marked with a light purple sector. Point positions are constructed as successive reflections, without printing numerical coordinates or an angle value.
spec.mathematics: P1 is the reflection of P0 in the horizontal line. P2 is the reflection of P1 in the second line. All three points have equal distance from O.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the source givens O, theta, P0, P1 and P2 are visible.

inlines.text: Choose two reflection lines through the required centre, separated by half the required rotation angle. Their order determines the direction.

answer.worked:
Label the rising reflection ray $OA$ and the horizontal reflection ray $OB$. Reflection preserves distance from $O$, so $OP_0=OP_1=OP_2$. By reflection symmetry,
$$\begin{align*}
\angle AOP_2&=\angle AOP_1,\\
\angle BOP_0&=\angle BOP_1,\\
\angle AOP_1+\angle BOP_1&=\theta,\\
\angle P_0OP_2&=2(\angle AOP_1+\angle BOP_1),\\
\angle P_0OP_2&=2\theta.
\end{align*}$$
Thus the two reflections give a rotation through $2\theta$ anticlockwise about $O$ in the order shown. The same reflection-angle relationship applies to every point.

For any required rotation, choose two lines through its centre separated by half its angle. Reflect in the lines in the order giving the required direction.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Similarly, every translation can be achieved with two reflections. To show this, consider two parallel lines separated by distance $d$. A point $P_0$ is reflected in the first line to $P_1$ and then in the second line to $P_2$. Show that this is a translation by finding the translation distance. Explain why this implies any translation can be achieved with two reflections.

spec.description: Two vertical dashed parallel reflection lines, dimension d between them, and three collinear labelled successive point images. No numerical lengths or coordinates are printed.
spec.mathematics: P0 and P1 have equal perpendicular distances from the first line. P1 and P2 have equal perpendicular distances from the second line.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied points, reflection lines and separation d.

inlines.text: , perpendicular to the lines, from the first line towards the second.
For a required distance, choose parallel reflection lines perpendicular to the translation direction and separated by half that distance.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the perpendicular distance from $P_0$ to the first reflection line. Reflection puts $P_1$ at distance $x$ on its other side. In the diagram, $P_1$ is therefore $d-x$ from the second line, and $P_2$ is the same distance beyond it.
$$\begin{align*}
P_0P_2&=x+x+(d-x)+(d-x),\\
P_0P_2&=2d.
\end{align*}$$
Every point moves the same distance $2d$, perpendicular to the reflection lines and from the first line towards the second. Thus the composition is a translation.

For a translation of distance $L$, choose two parallel lines perpendicular to its direction and separated by $L/2$. Reflect first in the line behind the other in the required direction, then in the second line.

content.prompt: Prove that $\triangle ABC$ is an equilateral triangle if and only if $\angle A=\angle B=\angle C$. Hint: An equilateral triangle is an isosceles triangle.

answer.short:
Equal angles give equal opposite sides, so the triangle is equilateral. Conversely, equal sides give equal opposite angles.

Apply AAS and RHS to pairs of triangles formed by altitudes to prove these equalities.
answer.worked:
Suppose $\angle A=\angle B=\angle C$. Draw the altitude $AD$ to $BC$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle ABD&=\angle ACD &&\text{(given)}\\\angle ADB&=\angle ADC=90^\circ &&\text{(altitude)}\\AD&=AD &&\text{(shared side)}\end{align*}$$
Thus $\triangle ABD\cong\triangle ACD$ by AAS, so $AB=AC$. Similarly, draw the altitude from $B$ to $AC$. The resulting right triangles are congruent by AAS because $\angle A=\angle C$ and the altitude is shared. Hence $AB=BC$. Therefore $AB=BC=CA$, so $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral.

Conversely, suppose $AB=BC=CA$. Draw the altitude $AD$ to $BC$.
$$\begin{align*}AB&=AC &&\text{(equilateral triangle)}\\AD&=AD &&\text{(shared side)}\\\angle ADB&=\angle ADC=90^\circ &&\text{(altitude)}\end{align*}$$
Thus $\triangle ABD\cong\triangle ACD$ by RHS, so $\angle B=\angle C$. Similarly, an altitude from $C$ gives right triangles congruent by RHS, so $\angle A=\angle B$. Therefore $\angle A=\angle B=\angle C$.

answer.worked:
$\angle BAX=\angle EDY$, since $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle DEF$ and the altitude feet lie on the corresponding bases.

$\operatorname{area}(\triangle DEF)=k^2\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)$.

Corresponding bases and altitudes each have scale factor $k$, so each triangle formed by an altitude has area scale factor $k^2$. Add the two areas.
answer.worked:
From part (a), the scale factor between $\triangle ABX$ and $\triangle DEY$ is $DE/AB=k$. Thus $DY=kAX$ and $EY=kBX$.

$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{area}(\triangle DEF)&=\operatorname{area}(\triangle DEY)+\operatorname{area}(\triangle FEY)\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle DEF)&=k^2\bigl(\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABX)+\operatorname{area}(\triangle CBX)\bigr)\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle DEF)&=k^2\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC).\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$4\sqrt{3}-6$.

Use the similar triangle above the square and the triangle's height $\sqrt{3}$.
answer.worked:
Let $s$ be the square's side length. The altitude bisects the equilateral triangle's base, so its height $H$ satisfies
$$\begin{align*}
H^2&=2^2-1^2\\
H&=\sqrt{3}.
\end{align*}$$
The triangle above the square is similar to the whole triangle (AAA similarity), since the square's top edge is parallel to the base. Their bases are $s$ and $2$, and their heights are $\sqrt{3}-s$ and $\sqrt{3}$.
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{s}{2}&=\frac{\sqrt{3}-s}{\sqrt{3}}\\
\sqrt{3}s&=2\sqrt{3}-2s\\
(\sqrt{3}+2)s&=2\sqrt{3}\\
s&=\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{2+\sqrt{3}}\\
s&=\frac{2\sqrt{3}(2-\sqrt{3})}{(2+\sqrt{3})(2-\sqrt{3})}\\
s&=4\sqrt{3}-6.
\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$\triangle ABD\sim\triangle CB'C'$ (AAA).

Reflection preserves $\angle B$, and $C'C\parallel AD$ gives the second matching angle.
answer.worked:
Reflection preserves angles, so $\angle CB'C'=\angle ABC=\angle ABD$, since $B',A,C$ are collinear and $D$ lies on $BC$.

Also, $C'C\parallel AD$ because both are perpendicular to the reflection axis. Therefore $\angle B'CC'=\angle CAD=\angle BAD$, since $AD$ bisects $\angle A$.

The remaining angles are equal by the angle sum of a triangle. Hence $\triangle ABD\sim\triangle CB'C'$ (AAA similarity).

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, prove the Angle Bisector Theorem.

answer.short:
$\displaystyle\frac{BD}{CD}=\frac{AB}{AC}$.

Use corresponding-side ratios, then $CB'=AB+AC$ and $B'C'=BC=BD+CD$.
answer.worked:
From part (a), corresponding sides are proportional. Reflection gives $B'C'=BC$ and $AB'=AB$. Since $B',A,C$ are collinear, $CB'=AB+AC$.

$$\begin{align*}
\frac{AB}{CB'}&=\frac{BD}{B'C'}\\
\frac{AB}{AB+AC}&=\frac{BD}{BD+CD}\\
\frac{AB+AC}{AB}&=\frac{BD+CD}{BD}\\
1+\frac{AC}{AB}&=1+\frac{CD}{BD}\\
\frac{AC}{AB}&=\frac{CD}{BD}\\
\frac{AB}{AC}&=\frac{BD}{CD}.
\end{align*}$$

Thus the Angle Bisector Theorem holds.

Repeat part (a) with top lengths $\dfrac1n$ and $1-\dfrac1n$.
answer.worked:
Use the same point names as in part (a), with $AB=1/n$ and $CB=1-1/n$. Pythagoras in $\triangle ABE$ gives
$$\begin{align*}x^2+\frac1{n^2}&=(1-x)^2,\\x^2+\frac1{n^2}&=1-2x+x^2,\\2x&=1-\frac1{n^2},\\x&=\frac{n^2-1}{2n^2}.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\frac{AB}{CD}&=\frac{AE}{CB},\\\frac{1/n}{y}&=\frac{x}{1-1/n},\\y&=\frac{n-1}{n^2x},\\y&=\frac{2(n-1)}{n^2-1},\\y&=\frac2{n+1}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Prove that the following are equivalent properties of a quadrilateral; that is, prove that any one of these properties implies the other three.

children.label: a
children.prompt: The quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

answer.short:
Property (a) implies property (b).

Draw $BD$. Alternate angles and the shared diagonal give $\triangle ABD\equiv\triangle CDB$ by AAS, so opposite sides are equal.
answer.worked:
Let the quadrilateral be $ABCD$. We prove the cycle (a), (b), (c), (d), then (a); following this cycle shows that any one property implies the other three.

Assume (a) and draw $BD$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle ABD&=\angle CDB &&\text{(alternate angles, }AB\parallel CD\text{)}\\\angle ADB&=\angle CBD &&\text{(alternate angles, }AD\parallel BC\text{)}\\BD&=DB &&\text{(shared side)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle ABD\equiv\triangle CDB$ by AAS. Corresponding sides give $AB=CD$ and $AD=CB$, establishing (b).

children.label: b
children.prompt: The opposite sides have equal length.

answer.short:
Property (b) implies property (c).

SSS congruence across each diagonal gives equal opposite angles.
answer.worked:
Assume (b). Draw $BD$ and $AC$.
$$\begin{align*}AB&=CD &&\text{(given)}\\AD&=CB &&\text{(given)}\\BD&=DB &&\text{(shared side)}\end{align*}$$
Thus $\triangle ABD\equiv\triangle CDB$ by SSS, so $\angle BAD=\angle DCB$.

Also $AB=CD$, $BC=DA$ and $AC=CA$, so $\triangle ABC\equiv\triangle CDA$ by SSS. Hence $\angle ABC=\angle CDA$. Both pairs of opposite angles are equal, establishing (c).

children.label: c
children.prompt: The opposite angles have equal measure.

answer.short:
Property (c) implies property (d).

The angle sum gives supplementary adjacent angles, hence parallel opposite sides. AAS congruence at the diagonal intersection shows that both diagonals are bisected.
answer.worked:
Assume (c), so $\angle A=\angle C$ and $\angle B=\angle D$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle A+\angle B+\angle C+\angle D&=360^\circ\\2\angle A+2\angle B&=360^\circ\\\angle A+\angle B&=180^\circ\\\angle B+\angle C&=180^\circ\end{align*}$$
The converse of the co-interior angle result gives $AD\parallel BC$ and $AB\parallel CD$. Thus $ABCD$ is a parallelogram, and the proof in (a) gives $AB=CD$.

Let $X$ be the intersection of $AC$ and $BD$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle BAX&=\angle DCX &&\text{(alternate angles)}\\\angle ABX&=\angle CDX &&\text{(alternate angles)}\\AB&=CD &&\text{(opposite sides of a parallelogram)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle BXA\equiv\triangle DXC$ by AAS. Corresponding sides give $AX=CX$ and $BX=DX$. Hence the diagonals bisect each other, establishing (d).

children.label: d
children.prompt: The diagonals bisect each other.

answer.short:
Property (d) implies property (a).

SAS congruence at the diagonal intersection gives equal alternate angles, so both pairs of opposite sides are parallel. The completed cycle proves all four properties equivalent.
answer.worked:
Assume (d), and let $X$ be the intersection of $AC$ and $BD$.
$$\begin{align*}AX&=CX &&\text{(given)}\\BX&=DX &&\text{(given)}\\\angle AXB&=\angle CXD &&\text{(vertically opposite angles)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle AXB\equiv\triangle CXD$ by SAS. Hence $\angle BAX=\angle DCX$, so $AB\parallel CD$ by the converse of the alternate-angle result.

Similarly, $BX=DX$, $CX=AX$ and $\angle BXC=\angle DXA$, so $\triangle BXC\equiv\triangle DXA$ by SAS. Thus $\angle CBX=\angle ADX$, giving $BC\parallel AD$.

Therefore $ABCD$ is a parallelogram, establishing (a). The cycle is complete, so each property implies the other three.

children.prompt: Prove that the base angles of an isosceles trapezium have the same measure.

The angles on each non-parallel side are supplementary:
$$\begin{align*}\angle ABC&=180^\circ-\angle BAD\\\angle BCD&=180^\circ-\angle CDA.\end{align*}$$
Hence $\angle ABC=\angle BCD$ as well.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Prove that a trapezium whose base angles have the same measure is an isosceles trapezium.

answer.short:
$AB=CD$, so $ABCD$ is an isosceles trapezium.

Perpendicular constructions give congruent right triangles by AAS.
answer.worked:
Draw $BE\perp AD$ and $CF\perp AD$, with $E,F$ on $AD$. Since $BC\parallel AD$, $BE=CF$. The given equal base angles give $\angle BAE=\angle CDF$, and $\angle AEB=\angle DFC=90^\circ$.

Therefore $\triangle ABE\equiv\triangle DCF$ by AAS. Corresponding sides give $AB=CD$, so $ABCD$ is an isosceles trapezium.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Prove that the diagonals of an isosceles trapezium have the same length.

answer.short:
$BD=AC$.

Use the equal base angles to prove $\triangle BAD\equiv\triangle CDA$ by SAS.
answer.worked:
Draw diagonals $BD$ and $AC$. In $\triangle BAD$ and $\triangle CDA$:
$$\begin{align*}AB&=CD&&\text{(given)}\\AD&=DA&&\text{(shared side)}\\\angle BAD&=\angle CDA&&\text{(part a)}.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle BAD\equiv\triangle CDA$ by SAS. Corresponding sides give $BD=AC$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Prove that a trapezium with diagonals of the same length is an isosceles trapezium.

answer.short:
$AB=CD$, so $ABCD$ is an isosceles trapezium.

Similarity at the diagonal intersection gives $AX=DX$; then use SAS congruence.
answer.worked:
Let the equal diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meet at $X$. Since $AD\parallel BC$, alternate angles give $\angle XAD=\angle XCB$ and $\angle XDA=\angle XBC$. Therefore $\triangle AXD\sim\triangle CXB$ by AA.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{BX}{DX}&=\frac{CX}{AX}\\\frac{BX+DX}{DX}&=\frac{CX+AX}{AX}\\\frac{BD}{DX}&=\frac{AC}{AX}\\\frac{BD}{DX}&=\frac{BD}{AX}.\end{align*}$$
Hence $AX=DX$. The isosceles triangle $AXD$ gives $\angle XDA=\angle DAX$, so $\angle BDA=\angle CAD$.

Now $BD=CA$, $DA=AD$ and the included angles are equal. Thus $\triangle BDA\equiv\triangle CAD$ by SAS. Corresponding sides give $AB=CD$, so $ABCD$ is an isosceles trapezium.

content.prompt: Suppose $\triangle ABC$ is a right-angled triangle. Denote the side lengths by $a$, $b$ and $c$ where $c$ is the hypotenuse. Determine the value of the inradius in terms of $a$, $b$ and $c$.

answer.worked:
Draw radii from the incentre to the three points of tangency. Each radius is perpendicular to its side. At the right-angle vertex, the two radii and the two tangent segments form a square, so both tangent segments have length $r.$

The remaining segments on the legs have lengths $a-r$ and $b-r$. Tangent segments from the same vertex are equal, as follows from RHS congruence of the right triangles formed by the radii and the line to that vertex. Thus the hypotenuse consists of segments of lengths $a-r$ and $b-r$.
$$\begin{align*}c&=(a-r)+(b-r)\\c&=a+b-2r\\2r&=a+b-c\\r&=\frac{a+b-c}{2}.\end{align*}$$

In an equilateral triangle, each altitude is both an angle bisector and a perpendicular bisector of the opposite side. Thus the incentre and circumcentre coincide. On an altitude, the distance from this centre to the base is $r$, and its distance to the opposite vertex is $R$.

$$\begin{align*}R&=h-r\\R&=\frac{\sqrt{3}a}{2}-\frac{a}{2\sqrt{3}}\\R&=\frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Prove that the circumcentre and incentre of a triangle are the same point if and only if the triangle is equilateral.

answer.short:
In an equilateral triangle, each altitude is both a perpendicular bisector and an angle bisector, so the centres coincide.

Conversely, a common centre has equal distances to the vertices and equal perpendicular distances to the sides. RHS congruence makes the six resulting right triangles congruent, so all three sides are equal.
answer.worked:
Suppose $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral. Draw the altitude $AD$ to $BC$. In $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle ACD$,
$$\begin{align*}AB&=AC &&\text{(equilateral triangle)}\\AD&=AD &&\text{(shared side)}\\\angle ADB&=\angle ADC=90^\circ &&\text{(altitude)}.\end{align*}$$
Thus $\triangle ABD\equiv\triangle ACD$ by RHS. Corresponding sides give $BD=CD$, and corresponding angles give $\angle BAD=\angle DAC$. Hence $AD$ is both the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ and the bisector of $\angle A$. The same argument applies at the other vertices. Therefore the perpendicular bisectors and angle bisectors have the same intersection, so the circumcentre and incentre coincide.

Conversely, suppose the circumcentre and incentre coincide at $O$. Let $D$, $E$ and $F$ be the perpendicular feet from $O$ to $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$, respectively. Since $O$ is the circumcentre and incentre,
$$\begin{align*}OA&=OB=OC,\\OD&=OE=OF.\end{align*}$$
The six right triangles $\triangle AOF$, $\triangle AOE$, $\triangle BOF$, $\triangle BOD$, $\triangle COD$ and $\triangle COE$ are congruent by RHS: their hypotenuses are equal and their perpendicular legs are equal. Their remaining legs are therefore equal:
$$AF=AE=BF=BD=CD=CE.$$
Each side of $\triangle ABC$ is the sum of two of these equal lengths. Thus $AB=BC=CA$, so the triangle is equilateral.

answer.short: Use strong induction. The altitude construction gives four pieces. A non-equilateral triangle can be cut into one isosceles triangle and another triangle. For an equilateral triangle, a centre construction gives five pieces; for larger totals, retain two centre triangles and subdivide the third.
answer.worked:
First draw an altitude from the vertex opposite a longest side. It produces two right-angled triangles. By part (a), each can be split into two isosceles triangles, proving the case $n=4$.

Any non-equilateral triangle has a vertex with unequal adjacent sides. Mark a point on the longer side at a distance from this vertex equal to the shorter side, and join it to the opposite vertex. This cuts off one isosceles triangle and leaves another triangle.

We must separately establish five pieces for an equilateral triangle $ABC$. Join its centre $O$ to $A,B,C$, forming three isosceles triangles with centre angles $120^\circ$. In $\triangle OAB$, take $D$ on $AB$ so that $OD\perp OB$. Then $\angle OAD=30^\circ$ and $\angle AOD=120^\circ-90^\circ=30^\circ$, so $\triangle AOD$ is isosceles. Triangle $ODB$ is right-angled and splits into two isosceles triangles by part (a). Along with $OBC$ and $OCA$, this gives five pieces. For a non-equilateral triangle, the preceding cut and the four-piece construction on the remaining triangle also give five pieces.

Now use strong induction. Assume every triangle can be decomposed into $k$ isosceles triangles for each $4\leq k<n$, where $n\geq6$. For a non-equilateral triangle, cut off one isosceles triangle and divide the remaining triangle into $n-1$ pieces by the hypothesis. For an equilateral triangle, join its centre to its vertices and retain two of the resulting isosceles triangles. The third triangle can be divided into $n-2$ pieces, since $4\leq n-2<n$. Both cases give $n$ pieces. Therefore every triangle can be decomposed into $n$ isosceles triangles for every integer $n\geq4$.
